issues.legal_issue: A suit for eviction validly instituted after the required permission has been obtained remains maintainable when the State Government later revokes that permission.
material_facts: The landlord obtained permission from the District Magistrate to sue for eviction, and the tenant’s revision to the Commissioner was dismissed.
The landlord filed the eviction suit before the State Government decided the tenant’s further revision.
After the suit was filed, the State Government set aside the Commissioner’s order and revoked the permission to sue.
issues.conclusion: The later revocation did not make the suit incompetent; the suit, validly instituted after the required permission, remained maintainable.
issues.legal_principle: Under sections 3(1)–(4) of the U.P. (Temporary) Control of Rent and Eviction Act, 1947, institution of a suit outside the specified grounds required the District Magistrate’s permission, which was expressly subject to revision by the Commissioner, but section 3(1) did not make institution subject to a later order under section 7-F. Section 7-F permits revision before the suit is instituted and does not invalidate a suit already filed; absent statutory language making a decree inexecutable or reopening proceedings, a validly instituted suit must take its course. Bhagwan Das v. Paras Nath was followed; Shri Bhagwan v. Ram Chand and Bansi Ram v. Mantri Lal were considered.

predicates.eviction_suit_proceeding: A landlord brought a proceeding seeking eviction of a tenant.
predicates.required_permission_obtained: The landlord obtained the permission required to institute the eviction suit, including the relevant review by the intermediate authority.
predicates.suit_filed_before_state_revision_decisio: The landlord filed the suit before the State Government decided the further revision concerning permission.

issues.definition: When a landlord brings an eviction suit after obtaining the required permission and files it before the State Government decides a further revision, a later revocation of permission does not defeat the suit.

issues.legal_issue: The statutory bar on questioning administrative orders in court does not prevent a court from setting aside an order made in breach of natural justice, but it prevents review of the order’s propriety when the authority properly exercised its jurisdiction.
material_facts: The tenant argued that the provision barring court challenges to orders made under the Act prevented a court from considering the State Government’s order.
The Court considered the effect of that bar and the scope of judicial scrutiny of an order made under the State Government’s revisionary power.
issues.conclusion: An order made in breach of natural justice may be quashed; where the State Government has properly exercised its jurisdiction, a court cannot examine the propriety of its order.
issues.legal_principle: Section 16 of the U.P. (Temporary) Control of Rent and Eviction Act, 1947, does not exclude judicial review of an order made in violation of natural justice. However, once the jurisdiction under that section is properly exercised, the court cannot examine the order’s propriety. Shri Bhagwan v. Ram Chand was considered.

predicates.challenge_to_administrative_order: A party asked a court to review an order made by an administrative authority under the governing rent-control scheme.
predicates.order_made_without_reasonable_opportunit: The authority made its order without giving both affected parties a reasonable opportunity to be heard.

issues.definition: When a party challenges an administrative order and the authority made it without giving both affected parties a reasonable opportunity to be heard, the order may be quashed.
